case_title: Badal Murmu and Ors. v. State of West Bengal
accused_socioeconomic_status: Very poor; described as economically so weak that possession of a hen is very important to them
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (fellow villagers of the same community)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148; IPC s.302 r/w s.149 (conviction altered to IPC s.304 Part II)
weapon: Lathis (sticks); tangies (sharp cutting weapons) were carried but not used
aggravating_circumstances: Death from repeated lathi blows; fourteen injuries including two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp
mitigating_circumstances: Trivial triggering dispute; no sharp weapon used despite availability; poor tribal accused; long time in custody
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.148 and s.302 r/w s.149; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (IPC s.304 Part II)
neutral_facts: A hen belonging to one of the accused was stolen and killed by the victim. A community tribunal (salish) ordered the victim to give a hen and two handies of liquor as a penalty, and the penalty was paid. The previous day, the victim and a second man were discussing the matter when one of the accused overheard them and objected. The second man was assaulted with sticks and later examined by a doctor. The next morning, the victim and the second man were summoned to a courtyard on the pretext of a meeting about the incident. There the second man was tied to a tree and the victim to a bamboo pole. A group of men armed with sticks and sharp cutting tools then assaulted them. The second man managed to escape. The men continued beating the victim with sticks until he died. Two wives of the victim, who had followed him to the courtyard, saw the assault. Women present also assaulted the victim's wives, mother and sister. The first wife went to the police station and gave a statement naming all the men as assailants, and an investigation followed. The first wife, the victim's sister, the second wife and the second man gave evidence describing the assault. None of them said which man struck which blow. The post-mortem doctor recorded fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, along with two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp. The doctor stated that all the injuries contributed to death and that a blunt object such as a lathi could cause them. The doctor did not identify any particular fatal injury. Some of the men carried sharp cutting tools but did not use them.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, plus two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp
number_of_offences: 2 charged; 1 finally upheld (IPC s.304 Part II). The s.148 conviction is not expressly addressed in the judgment
financial_property_loss: Earlier theft of a hen from the accused; penalty of one hen and two handies of liquor paid by the victim
premeditation_planning: Not found. The court held there was no shared common object to kill; the lathi blows were struck in a frenzy
motive: Anger at the penalty imposed by the community tribunal over the theft of a hen (court's finding, with the mitigating context that it was a trivial dispute)
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular testimony of PW-1, PW-3, PW-6 and PW-7; post-mortem evidence of PW-9 that the injuries could be caused by a blunt object like a lathi
witness_credibility: Truthful and reliable. The witnesses were rustic and candid. They were related to the deceased, but the court found it not possible to say they falsely implicated the accused. PW-7 named his own brother as an assailant
custody_duration: Almost 14 years, as informed to the court
trial_duration: offence: not given (the fatal assault occurred the day after 14/4/1989); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 20.01.2003; Supreme Court: 5 February 2014
legal_representation: Accused: Ms. Vibha Datta Makhija (amicus curiae, with Ruchi Agnihotri). State: Anip Sachthey, Kabir S. Bose, Shagun Matta, Saakaar Sardana
investigation_status: Complaint lodged at police station by the first wife; investigation completed; accused charged; 10 prosecution witnesses examined
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.148 and s.302 r/w s.149 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: conviction altered to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (s.304 Part II); sentence treated as time already undergone
prosecution_argument: The ocular evidence proves the case. Even if the common object was only to inflict injuries, every member of the unlawful assembly knew murder was likely, so all should be held guilty of murder. The repeated assault and grievous injuries show intention to murder
defence_argument: Prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, so acquittal is sought. Alternatively, the offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s.304 Part II because lathis were used, the injuries are superficial and not on vital parts, and the accused are poor tribals who have been in jail for a long time
legal_principle_applied: Common object under s.149 must be established on the facts; individual roles and the fatal injury must be considered; where there is no intention to kill and the injuries are non-fatal or not individually attributed, s.304 Part II applies
precedent_relied_upon: Sukhdev Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1992 SC 755); Sarman & Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1993 Supp. (2) SCC 356); Kirti Mahto & Ors. v. State of Bihar (1994 Supp. (2) SCC 569); Molu & Ors. v. State of Haryana (AIR 1976 SC 2499); Munivel v. State of Tamil Nadu ((2006) 9 SCC 394); Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra ((2012) 2 SCC 648); Kashmiri Lal & Ors. v. State of Punjab (AIR 1997 SC 393)
sentencing_rationale: Trivial triggering incident; the accused's anger at the theft must be seen against their poverty and social status; no intention to kill; long period already spent in jail; convicting under s.304 Part II and treating time served as sentence meets the ends of justice
judicial_mitigating_factors: Trivial cause of the incident; poor tribal background and social status; no shared intention to kill; sharp weapons available but not used; about 14 years in jail
judicial_aggravating_factors: None weighed as aggravating; the court noted no justification for the assault but did not treat any factor as aggravating
other_sentence_order: Accused directed to be released forthwith unless required in any other case
